author: Mark Atwood
text:
Decided: we support 1970-2049. Not a fork of der, and not an open limitation any more -- a stated scope boundary.

Reframed accordingly in pkix-path's rustdoc and README. It no longer reads as 'der won't let us' but as the decision it is: the floor is the Unix epoch because der 0.8 puts it there, lifting it means forking the DER layer every consumer of this workspace builds against, and no conforming CA issues certificates dated before 1970. The trade is a fork of a foundational dependency against twenty years of dates nobody uses.

The README gained a 'Supported date range' section, since this is something a consumer needs to know up front rather than find in Limitations.

Pinned with tests (pkix-path/tests/utctime_range.rs) so the boundary cannot move unnoticed in either direction -- if a dependency bump widens the range, the first test fails and the documented range has to be updated with it.

The second test is the one worth having: it proves the boundary is the EPOCH, not the millennium. That is the mistake this workspace actually made -- baseline-pkits-analysis.md described the limit as 'pre-2000 UTCTime' for several revisions. Invalidpre2000UTCEEnotAfterDateTest7EE is named 'pre2000', is dated 1997-1999, and parses fine; pre2000CRLnextUpdateCACert is 2010 and parses. Only the 1950 fixture is refused. A test that checked only the 1950 case would pass equally under a parser that rejected everything before 2000.

Fail-closed either way: such a certificate is refused, never misread. PKITS 4.2.3 stays the one vector this crate does not evaluate, and that is now documented as expected rather than outstanding.
